passages.title: Victory arrives, so praise and seek forgiveness
passages.tafsir:
# Sūrah An-Naṣr 110:1–3 — Victory arrives, so praise and seek forgiveness

These three ayat describe a single moment: Allah's help arrives, Makkah is opened, and whole peoples pour into Islam — and at exactly that moment the Prophet ﷺ is told not to celebrate but to glorify his Lord and seek forgiveness. What holds the passage together is that structure: ayat 1 and 2 are the condition ("when… and when you see…"), and ayah 3 is the response ("so glorify… and seek forgiveness"). Everything hinges on the strangeness of that response. And beneath the surface, as the Companions came to understand, the whole passage is a farewell.

## The last complete sūrah revealed

An-Nasa'i recorded that Ibn 'Abbās asked 'Ubaydullāh bin 'Abdullāh bin 'Utbah which sūrah of the Qur'an was revealed last. He answered, "*Idhā jā'a naṣru-llāhi wal-fatḥ*," and Ibn 'Abbās said, "You have spoken truthfully."

Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān notes that Sahih Muslim records the same from Ibn 'Abbās (as cited by Qurtubī), and clarifies what this means precisely: this was the last *complete* sūrah revealed. Individual verses came down afterwards, and that is no contradiction — just as Sūrah Al-Fātiḥah is called the first sūrah revealed even though scattered verses of Al-'Alaq, Al-Muddaththir and others preceded it. "First" and "last" here mean the first and last sūrahs revealed *whole*.

Ma'ārif also records that the scholars agree this sūrah was revealed in Madinah, and that it carries a second name: **Sūrah At-Tawdī'** — *tawdī'* meaning "to bid farewell." It is called that because it signals the approach of the Prophet's ﷺ departure; the sūrah bids him farewell. Ibn Kathīr also mentions that it has been said this sūrah is equivalent to one-fourth of the Qur'an, as is Sūrah Az-Zalzalah.

## The gathering of the elders of Badr

The single most illuminating thing about this passage is a scene Al-Bukhārī recorded from Ibn 'Abbās, and it is worth telling in full.

'Umar used to bring the young Ibn 'Abbās into his gatherings with the veterans of Badr. One of them resented it: "Why do you bring this boy to sit with us when we have children his age?" 'Umar replied, "He is among those whom you know." Then one day 'Umar called them together and invited Ibn 'Abbās — and Ibn 'Abbās says he does not think 'Umar invited him that day except to show them.

'Umar asked the gathering: "What do you say about Allah's statement, *When there comes the help of Allah and the Conquest*?"

Some of them said: "We were commanded to praise Allah and seek His forgiveness when He helps us and gives us victory." Others said nothing at all.

Then 'Umar turned to Ibn 'Abbās: "Is this what you say?"

"No."

"Then what do you say?"

Ibn 'Abbās said: "**It was the end of the life of Allah's Messenger ﷺ that Allah was informing him of.** *When there comes the help of Allah and the Conquest* — that is a sign of the end of your life. *So glorify the praises of your Lord, and ask His forgiveness. Verily, He is the One Who accepts repentance.*"

And 'Umar said: "I do not know anything about it other than what you have said."

Ibn Kathīr notes that Al-Bukhārī was alone in recording this ḥadīth. Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān mentions the same account from Sahih Bukhari, adding the detail that when 'Umar heard Ibn 'Abbās's explanation, he concurred with him.

Notice how the exchange runs. The elders answered with the surface of the words — and that answer, taken on its own, is what the words plainly say. But Ibn 'Abbās, asked directly whether that was his own view, said simply "No," and read the passage differently: why is a man told to seek forgiveness at the summit of his mission, unless the mission is complete and the return is near? And 'Umar — the one who had convened the gathering — set the first answer aside and took the young man's. Mission accomplished means it is time to go home.

Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān records another version, from Muqātil's narration: when this sūrah was revealed the Prophet ﷺ recited it before a gathering of Companions including Abū Bakr, 'Umar, and Sa'd ibn Abī Waqqāṣ. All of them rejoiced — it carried the glad tidings of the conquest of Makkah — but 'Abbās began to weep. When the Prophet ﷺ asked him why, he said it quietly announces the ending of your life and that your death is near. And the Prophet ﷺ confirmed it.

Imām Aḥmad recorded from Ibn 'Abbās that when this ayah was revealed, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: **"My death has been announced to me."** And he died during that year. Ibn Kathīr notes that Aḥmad was alone in recording this ḥadīth.

## "Al-Fatḥ" — which victory?

Ibn Kathīr is unambiguous: the meaning of *al-Fatḥ* here is the conquest of Makkah, and there is only one view concerning it. Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān agrees — there is complete unanimity on this historical fact.

Note the definite article. Not *a* victory but **the** Victory — the promised one, the one everything had been building towards.

The word *naṣr* is Allah's help, and the ayah is precise: *naṣru-llāh*, **Allah's** help. The triumph is attributed to its true source before it is described at all. Nothing in ayah 1 belongs to the one receiving it.

**When was it revealed?** Here the scholars genuinely differ, and Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān lays out the disagreement rather than settling it:

- The phrase *idhā jā'a* — "when there comes" — apparently indicates the sūrah was revealed *before* the Conquest, since it speaks of something still to arrive. Rūḥ-ul-Ma'ānī cites a narration from Al-Baḥr-ul-Muḥīṭ agreeing with this, stating the sūrah came down while returning from the expedition of Khaybar — and the victory of Khaybar is known to have preceded the Conquest of Makkah. Rūḥ-ul-Ma'ānī also cites, on the authority of 'Abd ibn Ḥumayd, Qatādah's statement that the Prophet ﷺ lived for two years after this sūrah was revealed.
- Other narrations place it at the Conquest itself, or at the Farewell Pilgrimage. Ma'ārif offers a way to reconcile them: the Prophet ﷺ may have recited and proclaimed this sūrah on those occasions, and people therefore understood it to have been revealed then.

Ma'ārif also records from Ibn 'Umar that this sūrah was revealed during the Farewell Pilgrimage, and that after it — and the revelation that shortly followed it — the Messenger of Allah ﷺ lived only eighty days. A few further verses came down in his remaining days, and after the last of them he lived twenty-one days, and according to Muqātil only seven, and then he passed away. (Cited via Qurtubī.) Read this way, this sūrah opens the final countdown of the Prophet's ﷺ life.

## Ayah 2: why the crowds came

*And you see the people entering Allah's religion in crowds* — *afwājan*, in throngs, multitudes, droves. Not one by one, but in groups.

Ibn Kathīr explains the mechanism. The various regions of Arabia were **waiting** for the conquest of Makkah before accepting Islam. They said: "If he ﷺ is victorious over his own people, then he is a true Prophet." Al-Bukhārī recorded in his Ṣaḥīḥ from 'Amr bin Salamah: "When Makkah was conquered, all of the people rushed to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ to profess their Islam. The various regions were delaying their acceptance of Islam until Makkah was conquered. The people used to say, 'Leave him and his people alone. If he is victorious over them he is a true Prophet.'"

So when Allah gave him victory over Makkah, they entered the religion of Allah in crowds. Ibn Kathīr adds that two years did not pass before the Arabian peninsula was laden with faith, and there did not remain a single Arab tribe that did not profess Islam.

Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān fills in the human texture: before the Conquest there were many who were nearly convinced of the truth of the Prophet ﷺ and of Islam, but were held back — some feared Quraysh's hostility, others hesitated for other reasons. The Conquest removed those obstacles. Seven hundred people from Yemen embraced the religion, joining the Prophet ﷺ; on the way they called the adhān and recited the Qur'an.

Note that ayah 2 says *and you **see*** — the Prophet ﷺ is addressed as a witness. What he had been sent with is placed before his own eyes, and the sight of it is itself the sign.

## Ayah 3: the command, and its strangeness

*So glorify the praises of your Lord, and seek His forgiveness. Verily, He is the One Who accepts repentance.*

Two commands. **Tasbīḥ** — Ma'ārif renders *fasabbiḥ bi ḥamdi rabbik* as "pronounce the purity and praise of your Lord": declaring Allah free of every deficiency, joined to *ḥamd*, praise. And **istighfār** — seeking forgiveness.

The pairing is the heart of the passage. Victory tempts a person to look at himself. *Sabbiḥ* turns the eyes upward: the purity and perfection are His. *Istaghfir* turns the eyes inward: whatever shortfall there was, it was mine. Between them there is no room left for self-congratulation. Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān puts it simply — the sūrah teaches the Prophet ﷺ the beautiful manners of asking Allah's forgiveness and offering constant praise and thanks to his Lord.

And the ayah closes by naming Allah **Tawwāb** — rendered in the sources as "the One Who accepts the repentance and Who forgives." The command to seek forgiveness comes with its own guarantee attached. You are not told to knock at a closed door.

## How the Prophet ﷺ lived it

The sources show us the command being enacted, which is the best commentary of all.

Al-Bukhārī recorded that 'Ā'ishah said the Messenger of Allah ﷺ used to say often in his bowing and prostrating: *"Subḥānaka-llāhumma rabbanā wa biḥamdika, allāhumma-ghfir lī"* — "Glory to You, O Allah, our Lord, and praise be to You. O Allah, forgive me." She said **he did this as his interpretation of the Qur'an** — that is, showing its implementation. Ibn Kathīr notes the rest of the group also recorded it except At-Tirmidhī. Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān records the same from 'Ā'ishah, citing Bukhārī: after this sūrah was revealed, whenever he ﷺ performed a prayer he would recite that very supplication.

Look closely at it: *Subḥānaka… wa biḥamdika… ighfir lī*. It is ayah 3, turned into a whisper in sujūd. He did not merely obey the command; he made it the rhythm of his prayer.

Imām Aḥmad recorded from Masrūq that 'Ā'ishah said he ﷺ used to say often towards the end of his life: *"Subḥāna-llāhi wa biḥamdih, astaghfiru-llāha wa atūbu ilayh"* — "Glory to Allah, and praise be unto Him. I seek Allah's forgiveness and I repent to Him." And he ﷺ said: **"Verily, my Lord informed me that I would see a sign in my Ummah, and commanded me that when I see it I should glorify His praises and seek His forgiveness, for He is the One Who accepts repentance. And indeed I have seen it"** — then he recited these three ayat. Ibn Kathīr notes Muslim also recorded this ḥadīth. Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān reports the same supplication from Umm Salamah, adding that he ﷺ used to say, "I have been commanded to do so," and would recite this sūrah as his evidence.

"**And indeed I have seen it.**" He recognised the sign in the crowds streaming toward him — and answered it with worship.

Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān records from Abū Hurayrah (via Qurtubī) that after this sūrah was revealed, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ exerted himself in the worship of Allah so immensely that his feet would swell. His response to being told his work was finished was to work harder.

## A tear in the same passage

Imām Aḥmad recorded from Abū 'Ammār that a neighbour of Jābir bin 'Abdullāh told him: he returned from a journey, Jābir came and greeted him, and he began telling Jābir about the divisions among the people and what they had started doing. Jābir wept, and said: "I heard the Messenger of Allah ﷺ saying, **'Verily, the people have entered into the religion of Allah in crowds, and they will also leave it in crowds.'**"

The very word of ayah 2 — *afwājan* — is turned around. Crowds are how they came in; crowds are how they can go out. Numbers are a gift, not a guarantee.

## Living it

The lesson the commentators draw from ayah 3 is not primarily about how to handle a win. It is about how to meet an ending. Ma'ārif ul Qur'ān gives the point its own heading: when the approach of death is sensed, one needs to exert oneself immensely in tasbīḥ and istighfār. That is exactly what the Prophet ﷺ did. Told his work was done, he answered with more prayer, more remembrance, more seeking of forgiveness — until his feet swelled.

And the supplication he chose is available to anyone: *Subḥānaka-llāhumma rabbanā wa biḥamdika, allāhumma-ghfir lī*. Say it in rukū' and sujūd, as he did — and you are, in 'Ā'ishah's words, interpreting the Qur'an with your body.

The passage ends where it began: with Allah. His help in ayah 1, His religion in ayah 2, His glory, His forgiveness, and His name *Tawwāb* in ayah 3. Nothing here belongs to us except the asking.
